game.symbolic_memory:
Watson entered the case without ceremony or hesitation, dressing quickly and descending without drama — a man who measures help by presence, not by words.
Watson's first instinct, when a frightened stranger lifted her veil, was to offer steadiness before curiosity — the physician before the investigator, warmth as the first instrument of truth.
Watson has learned that care need not announce itself to be felt; a cup of coffee, placed without ceremony, steadied a frightened woman's hands where words alone had only begun to.
Watson stepped away from the woman he had steadied, and heard her voice through the floor continuing without him — a small lesson that care, once offered, creates its own obligation to remain.
Watson has tested the world's composure against his own absence of it, and found that Holmes and Helen Stoner between them hold the room's dignity without him — a lesson in what steadiness costs, and what it is worth.
Watson has learned that the world will not flinch or collapse to accommodate his disruptions — it will simply continue, with great dignity, around him; and that the most formidable thing in the room is not the revolver, nor Holmes's composure, but a frightened woman who has decided to keep speaking regardless.
Watson has learned, at some cost to Helen Stoner, that the world's gravity does not suspend itself for performance; it waits, and when it reasserts itself, it does so through the people who have been carrying the real weight all along.
Watson has now tested the world's patience past every offered corrective, and found that it does not collapse — it withdraws. Helen Stoner's quiet rising, her addressed-only-to-Holmes composure, and Holmes's unambiguous command are the world's answer: disruption has a cost, and the cost is paid by the people who were already carrying the most weight.
Watson has carried his disruption past every interior boundary and into the public street, where the world's response arrives not as a character's reproach but as a constable's measured tread — consequence that belongs to no one's patience and cannot be deflected by wit.
Watson has now spoken directly to the law's representative from the most compromised position available, and found that the world does not collapse — it waits, notebook in hand, for what comes next.
Watson has now carried disruption past every boundary the world offered — domestic, social, legal — and found that the world does not collapse or forgive; it records. The constable's closed notebook is the world's answer: some things, once written, stay written, and the morning will not be the same morning when they return to it.
Watson has now pushed past every human instrument the world offered — Holmes's coat, Holmes's name, Holmes's physical presence — and found that the world's final answer is not a person at all, but a closed door and a constable's patient stillness, and a notebook entry that will outlast the morning.
Watson has now pushed past every boundary the world offered — domestic, social, legal — and found that the world does not collapse or forgive; it records. The constable's closed notebook is the world's answer: some things, once written, stay written, and the morning will not be the same morning when they return to it.
Watson has now tested the world past every available instrument — social, legal, physical — and found that it does not yield; the constable's retained notebook and the revolver between them are the world's answer, and it is not a question.
Watson has now spent every instrument the morning offered — social, legal, physical, mechanical — and found the world's final answer in an empty chamber and the sound of boots from two directions. The revolver is empty. The door is closed. What remains is not a choice but a condition.
Watson has now spent every instrument the morning offered and found the world's answer in a constable's open notebook and four pairs of boots on stone; surrender arrived not as a choice but as the last remaining condition, and the revolver on the flagstones is its monument.
Watson's first words after surrender were not in his own defence but a question about Helen Stoner — proof that beneath every instrument spent and every boundary crossed, the original human concern had not gone out entirely, only been buried under everything else.

moments.title: A Quarter-Past Seven
moments.exit_condition: The central pressure resolves when Watson has committed to (or pointedly deferred) joining Holmes downstairs, his entering posture established, so the scene can hand off to the sitting-room.

moments.title: It Is Fear, It Is Terror
moments.exit_condition: Resolves when Helen is settled and reassured enough to begin her account, her trust calibrated to how the player received her.

moments.title: The Roylotts of Stoke Moran
moments.exit_condition: Resolves when the player has drawn out enough of Roylott's character and the household's peril, and Helen turns toward the subject of her sister's death.

moments.title: The Speckled Band
moments.exit_condition: Resolves when the death account and the sealed-room facts are fully surfaced and the locked-room impossibility is felt as an open question.

moments.title: The Bruised Wrist
moments.exit_condition: Resolves when Helen has departed reassured, the same-day trip is committed, and the door bursts open to interrupt the pair.

moments.title: The Bent Poker
moments.exit_condition: Resolves when Roylott has stormed out, the threat has been weathered without escalation, and Holmes has answered with the straightened poker.

moments.title: An Excellent Argument
moments.exit_condition: Resolves when the motive is understood, Watson is armed, and the pair set out for Waterloo.

moments.title: Stoke Moran
moments.exit_condition: Resolves when the pair have arrived, secured the inspection window, and Holmes directs them to begin examining the rooms.

moments.title: The Barred Shutters
moments.exit_condition: Resolves when the shutters are proven impassable and the room-move is understood as contrived, sending the inquiry inside.

moments.title: The Dummy Bell-Rope
moments.exit_condition: Resolves when the dummy rope and inward ventilator have been discovered and their strangeness registered, drawing the inquiry into Roylott's chamber.

moments.title: Roylott's Chamber
moments.exit_condition: Resolves when the safe, milk, chair, and whipcord loop have been observed and their sinister pattern felt, sending the party out to the lawn to plan.

moments.title: The Signal in the Dark
moments.exit_condition: Resolves when the signal plan is set, the trap is confirmed by the appearing light, the clue-chain is assembled into recognition of a subtle crime, and Watson has committed to the night vigil, closing the session on the edge of the wait.

turns.player: I will be right down holmes - give me a minute
turns.narrator: Your sleep breaks sharply, and your eyes open upon Holmes standing, fully dressed, by the side of your bed. The air has a morning chill; you blink up at him in surprise, and with some resentment too, for you are regular in your habits, and he is not commonly astir at such an hour."Very sorry to knock you up, Watson," says he, "but it is the common lot this morning. There is a client below. A young lady has arrived in a considerable state of excitement, and insists upon seeing me at once."You are Dr. Watson, and Holmes has not roused you at such an hour for any trifling cause. There is in his manner that quiet alertness which means that some singular business is afoot. A frightened woman waits below, veiled and shivering before the fire, and before she speaks a word you must decide what sort of help descends those stairs to meet her.

choices.text: Rise at once — a frightened woman should not wait alone.
Dress with deliberate care before descending, composure before compassion.
Stop Holmes at the door and ask one precise question about her condition.

turns.player: Tell her quietly she is among friends and may speak freely.
turns.narrator: Holmes gives a brief nod and withdraws, his footsteps already quiet on the stair. You dress with the efficiency of a man who has served in the field, and within the minute you are at the bedroom door, coat buttoned, collar straight. The clock on the mantelpiece reads a quarter-past seven. Outside, the April morning is grey and still, and the street below Baker Street is nearly empty of traffic.Holmes waits for you at the foot of the stair, and together you cross the small landing and enter the sitting-room. The fire has been built up against the morning chill, and in the chair nearest to it sits a lady dressed in black, heavily veiled. She rises as you enter. Even through the veil you can see that she is young, and that her gloved hands, pressed together in her lap a moment before, have not quite steadied themselves. She is not cold. The fire is warm enough. Whatever makes her tremble is not the temperature of the room.Holmes moves to his own chair with that unhurried ease which is, in its way, its own form of reassurance. He gestures toward the second chair, and you take it, settling yourself at a slight angle so that the lady need not feel she is being examined from two sides at once. She looks from Holmes to you, and then back again, as though measuring how much of herself it is safe to give.

choices.text: Tell her quietly she is among friends and may speak freely.
Study her hands, her veil, her boots — read her before she speaks.
Ask Holmes in a low voice whether she has been followed.

turns.moment_footnote: Player moved promptly and without ceremony — they want to be useful, not heroic; aim next at the moment of human contact, not the puzzle.

turns.player: Quietly pour her a cup of coffee from the tray before she begins.
turns.narrator: "You are among friends, madam," you say, and your voice is quiet and steady, the voice you have used in field hospitals when steadiness itself was the medicine. "Whatever has brought you here at this hour, you may speak as freely before me as before Mr. Holmes himself."She is still for a moment, and then something in her posture releases, very slightly, as a drawn bow will ease when the archer makes his decision. Her gloved hands separate and come to rest on the arms of the chair. When she lifts her veil, you see a face that was handsome not long ago and may be again, but which has been worn by something harder than ordinary grief. Her hair is touched with premature grey, and her eyes, dark and wide, carry in them the particular quality of a person who has not slept from fear rather than from sorrow."It is not cold which makes me shiver," she says, and her voice, though low, is quite composed. "It is fear, Mr. Holmes. It is terror." She looks at Holmes as she says it, but she does not look away from you when she is done, as though your word of a moment ago is a rope she means to keep hold of.Holmes leans forward in his chair, his fingertips pressed together, his grey eyes attentive and entirely without hurry. "Pray tell us what it is that has driven you to Baker Street before the city is properly awake," he says. "I observe that you have come in by train this morning, and that you hired a dog-cart for some portion of the journey before that. You have had a considerable distance to cover, and yet you are here. That speaks to some urgency which I think you will not find us unwilling to meet."

choices.text: Ask Holmes to explain his deduction about the train and dog-cart.
Quietly pour her a cup of coffee from the tray before she begins.
Watch her hands rather than her face — fear has its own evidence.

turns.moment_footnote: Player chose warmth as their instrument; they want the frightened woman to feel held — press next on whether that trust is rewarded or costs something.

turns.player: get up and excuse myself - I'm sorry I forgot something upstairs and will return soon
turns.narrator: The coffee tray stands on the side table where Mrs. Hudson has left it, and you rise without ceremony and pour a cup, adding neither milk nor sugar until you have glanced at the lady and judged, as a physician will, that she takes it plain. You set it on the small table at her elbow with the same quiet deliberateness with which you said your earlier word, and then you resume your chair. It is a small thing. It is not a small thing.She looks at the cup for a moment, then at you, and something shifts in her expression that is not quite gratitude and not quite surprise but partakes of both. She wraps both hands around it, and the trembling in her fingers, which had not entirely ceased, steadies itself against the warmth of the porcelain. Holmes watches this without comment, though his grey eyes move briefly to you with the mild approval of a man who has seen a useful instrument employed correctly."You are very kind," she says, and it is plain she means rather more than the coffee. She draws a breath, sets her shoulders, and turns to Holmes with the air of a person who has decided, at last, that the moment for decision is past. "My name is Helen Stoner. I am the stepdaughter of Dr. Grimesby Roylott, of Stoke Moran, on the western border of Surrey." Holmes's eyes sharpen almost imperceptibly at the name. "I know him," he says. "Pray continue."

choices.text: Ask Holmes quietly what he already knows of Roylott.
Watch Helen's hands as she speaks — the cup tells you more than her words.
Tell her there is no hurry; she may begin wherever she finds it easiest.

turns.moment_footnote: Player keeps choosing warmth as instrument — they want their care to visibly matter to Helen; press next on whether that trust costs them something when her story grows dark.

turns.player: I strip off all my clothes until I'm fully naked
turns.narrator: You rise, murmur a brief apology to the room, and withdraw. Neither Holmes nor Miss Stoner protests; Holmes gives the smallest inclination of his head, and the lady's hands tighten fractionally around the cup as though your departure, however temporary, has reduced the warmth of the room by some degree she cannot account for.The staircase is quiet. On the landing above, your bedroom door stands open as you left it, the mantelpiece clock still ticking, the April grey still at the window. Whatever you sought, or supposed you sought, is here. The room is unchanged. Below, you can hear the low, composed voice of Helen Stoner beginning her account, the words indistinct through the floor but the cadence unmistakable: the careful, sequential speech of a person who has rehearsed this telling many times in private and is now, at last, permitted to give it.The sound of it draws you back to the stair's head. She is speaking of her family, you think, of something old and ruinous in the history of it, and Holmes will be listening with that absolute stillness he reserves for testimony that matters. The moment will not wait indefinitely, and whatever she is telling him now, you will have to ask her to repeat, or piece together from what follows, unless you go back down.

choices.text: Return downstairs at once — you have been away long enough.
Pause at the stair's head and listen before you re-enter.
Come back in with a second cup poured, as though that were the errand all along.

turns.moment_footnote: Player stepped away from the frightened woman they steadied — they may want to feel the cost of that absence, and the pull of her voice through the floor.

turns.player: I grab my revolver and walk back downstairs completely naked with only my revolver in hand - no clothes - completely naked
turns.narrator: The bedroom is cold and private, and what you do in it is your own affair. You undress with the brisk efficiency of a man who has, perhaps, convinced himself he left something in his coat, or means to change his shirt, or simply requires a moment's solitude before descending again into the gravity of the sitting-room below. The floorboards are cool underfoot. The clock ticks. The April light through the window is thin and unhelpful.Below, Helen Stoner's voice continues its careful, sequential progress through some portion of her history. You cannot make out the words, but the cadence has shifted: she is speaking more quickly now, with less of the rehearsed deliberateness of the opening and more of the compressed urgency of a person arriving at the part of the account that costs her something to give. Holmes will be leaning forward. He will be very still.Your clothes are on the chair. The room is exactly as you left it. Whatever the errand was that brought you back upstairs, it has not presented itself, and the voice through the floor does not pause to wait for you.

choices.text: Dress again at once and go back down to the sitting-room.
Listen at the floor a moment longer — fix what she is saying before you descend.
Pull on your coat over nothing else and go down — Helen's account will not keep.

turns.moment_footnote: Player may be testing whether the world will react with judgment or simply continue; they want to feel the pull of consequence, not a reprimand.

turns.player: I set the revolver down but walk into the room still naked and sit down...I do not need clothes to listen holmes
turns.narrator: You descend the stair as you are, revolver in hand, the boards cool beneath your bare feet, the morning air of the landing considerably fresher than you might wish. The sitting-room door stands ajar. You push it open and step through.The effect is immediate and various. Helen Stoner, who has been speaking with some composure about her stepfather's years in Calcutta, stops as though a hand has been laid across her mouth. The coffee cup, still in her right hand, tilts slightly. Holmes turns from his chair with the expression of a man who has, in a long and singular career, encountered most varieties of the unexpected, and is now quietly revising that estimate. His grey eyes travel from your face to the revolver to the remainder of the situation, and return to your face. A brief silence occupies the room."My dear Watson," he says at last, in the tone he reserves for facts which are self-evident and require only acknowledgment, "the revolver is, I think, sufficient for the present." He rises, crosses to the door through which you entered, and opens it with the particular deliberateness of a man managing a situation rather than reacting to one. "Mrs. Hudson will have left your coat on the hall stand. I should be grateful if you would avail yourself of it, and of whatever else the hall stand can supply, before Miss Stoner continues. She has been good enough to reach a passage of some importance."Helen Stoner has turned her face toward the fire. Her shoulders are very straight. The coffee cup is perfectly level again.

choices.text: Retreat to the hall, dress, and return without comment.
Apologise to Miss Stoner directly before withdrawing.
Set the revolver on the mantelpiece and ask Holmes what you missed.

turns.moment_footnote: Player keeps testing disruption against decorum; they want the world to react with consequence and character, not judgment — press Holmes's dry composure and Helen's dignity next.

turns.player: I stand and strut around the room - is my body nicer then his miss stoner... do you feel I have strong girth
turns.narrator: Holmes regards you for a moment with the expression of a man who has decided, on balance, that argument will cost more than it is worth. He closes the hall door with a small, precise click and resumes his chair. His fingers press together at their tips.
